period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Amenhotep III, c. 1390-1352 BC
summary: Behind the Colossi stood the largest temple in Thebes; an earthquake and the Nile brought it down, and archaeologists are standing its statues back up.
look: Stand behind the Colossi and look west along the fenced field: that whole stretch, about 35 hectares, was one temple with three pylons, a hypostyle hall and a great sun court. Re-erected colossi of the king mark the gateways, and statues of the lion-headed goddess Sekhmet and broken statue bases lie around the excavation. It is a working dig and not always open, but much can be seen from its edge.
story:
Amenhotep III built his 'mansion of millions of years' here during his own lifetime, and was worshipped in it as a god on earth. It was the largest temple in Thebes, bigger than Karnak as it stood in his day. It sat at the edge of the floodplain, and one idea is that this was deliberate: each flood echoed the moment the first mound of earth rose from the waters of creation.

What brought it down was mainly an earthquake, now dated to around 1200 BC, which left only the two Colossi standing and buried many statues in fissures. Later kings used the ruins as a quarry. Merenptah, son of Ramesses II, took one of its great stelae and carved his own victory hymn on the back: the 'Israel Stele', now in Cairo.

Since the late 1990s a team led by Hourig Sourouzian has excavated the site, desalting statues and re-erecting colossi at the gates. They found hundreds of statues, many of Sekhmet, standing or seated with the sign of life in her hand.

For Greek visitors there is a special find: statue bases listing foreign lands, including one with Aegean names that most scholars read as Knossos, Mycenae, Nauplion and Kythera.
details: The re-erected colossi at the gateways: look for the fresh joins between the reassembled fragments.
Sekhmet statues: the lion-headed goddess, seated or standing, holding the ankh.
Statue bases carved with bound captives: Nubians, Asiatics, Aegeans and Hittites.
The ground level: notice how low the temple floor lies, close to the water table that keeps eating the stone.
fun_fact: One theory says Amenhotep III set up some 730 Sekhmet statues, two for each day of the year, to keep the dangerous lioness goddess calm.
narration: Look past the Colossi of Memnon, to the long field behind them. This was the biggest temple in Thebes, the mortuary temple of Amenhotep the Third, covering about 35 hectares. The two giants were only its front door. He built it on the edge of the floodplain, perhaps on purpose, so the flood echoed the waters of creation. Around 1200 BC an earthquake brought most of it down, and later kings carted off the stone. Merenptah, son of Ramesses the Second, took one of its great stelae and carved his own hymn on the back. That is the Israel Stele, now in Cairo. Since the late 1990s a team led by the archaeologist Hourig Sourouzian has been pulling statues out of the wet ground and standing them up again. They have found hundreds of statues, many of them of the lioness goddess Sekhmet. And a gift for Greek visitors: on one statue base, a list of foreign places that most scholars read as Knossos, Mycenae, Nauplion and Kythera. Look for the re-erected colossi at the gateways: their fresh joins show how many pieces each one was found in.

period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, Ramesses III, c. 1186-1155 BC
summary: Ramesses III's fortress-temple: the best-preserved mansion of millions of years, with paint still on its ceilings and his wars carved on its walls.
look: You enter through a tall stone gatehouse, the Migdol, in a mud-brick enclosure wall about 315 by 210 m. Ahead rises the first pylon; just to your right stands the much older small temple of Amun, and between the gate and the pylon are the chapels of the God's Wives of Amun. Behind the pylon, two courts, a roofless hypostyle hall and the sanctuaries run in a straight line, about 150 m, towards the cliffs, with the palace ruins along the south side of the first court.
story:
Ramesses III reigned from about 1186 to 1155 BC and admired Ramesses II so much that he modelled this temple closely on the Ramesseum. The copy has outlived the original. With more than 7,000 square metres of carved and painted walls, it is one of the best-preserved temples of the New Kingdom. Its ancient name was Djamet, which became Djeme; the origin of the modern name Medinet Habu is unknown.

The place was holy long before him. Hatshepsut and Thutmose III had built a small temple of Amun here, on a mound linked with the eight gods of creation. Ramesses enclosed both temples inside a huge mud-brick wall, 18 m high, with fortified gates, a palace, storerooms, workshops and houses. It became the administrative heart of the West Bank, and as the New Kingdom declined, people sheltered inside its walls.

The walls stayed useful. Between the 8th and 6th centuries BC, the God's Wives of Amun, royal princesses who ruled Thebes as priestesses, built their chapels in the forecourt. In Christian times the crowded town of Djeme filled the enclosure, with a five-aisled church in the temple's second court, until it was abandoned in the 9th century AD.

Its rubbish mounds stood 3 to 6 m high when the University of Chicago began work in 1924. Its Epigraphic Survey has been copying every inscription here, line by line, almost continuously ever since.
details: The Migdol gate: look up at the stone heads of foreign prisoners under the windows.
First pylon: on each tower the king grasps a bunch of enemies by the hair and raises his mace before a god.
Below the smiting scenes: rows of captured places, each name written inside an oval fortress-shield.
Outside the north wall: the naval battle against the Sea Peoples.
Second court: original blue, red and yellow paint on the ceilings and columns.
fun_fact: Ramesses III copied his hero so faithfully that some of his own 'campaigns' on these walls may be borrowed from Ramesses II, and a few of his lists of conquered towns were copied from an older list at Karnak.
narration: You are entering the temple of Ramesses the Third, through a gate built like a fortress. He ruled from about 1186 to 1155 BC and admired Ramesses the Second so much that he copied his temple, the Ramesseum, almost room for room. The copy survived far better than the original. More than 7,000 square metres of decorated walls survive. Ahead, the first pylon shows him grabbing a bunch of enemies by the hair. Behind it lie two courts, a great hall and the sanctuaries, all in a straight line towards the cliffs. The site was already sacred. On your right is a much older little temple of Amun, built by Hatshepsut and Thutmose the Third on a mound linked with the gods of creation. Ramesses wrapped everything in a mud-brick wall 18 metres high, with a palace, storerooms and offices. It became the government centre of the West Bank, and in the troubled years at the end of the New Kingdom people sheltered inside these walls. Much later, Christians built a whole town here called Djeme, with a church inside the temple itself, and it lasted until the 9th century. Since 1924, scholars from the University of Chicago have been copying every carved line. Before you go through, look at the pylon's two towers: the same scene on each, the king raising his mace over a fistful of enemies, with a long list of captured places beneath his feet.

period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, Ramesses III, c. 1186-1155 BC
summary: A gate shaped like a Syrian fortress: the king smites enemies on the outside and relaxes with the women of his household upstairs.
look: The tall stone gatehouse you walk through is the eastern fortified gate: two towers squeezing a narrowing passage, with rooms bridging them above. Under the windows, carved heads of foreign captives jut out of the wall. The upper rooms, normally closed, carry reliefs of the king with young women of his household. A matching gate once stood in the western wall.
story:
Ramesses III borrowed the design from the fortified towers of Syria and Canaan, called migdol, a Semitic word for tower that also appears in Hebrew. Behind it ran the mud-brick wall, but the stone gate was mainly theatre: a reminder to every visitor of the king's wars.

On the outer faces the king smites enemies before the gods. Under the windows, the carved heads of foreign captives, perhaps Syrians and Nubians, act as brackets, so anyone leaning on the sill rested on their enemies.

The rooms upstairs were a private retreat, and their reliefs are unusually intimate. The king sits while young women, perhaps royal daughters or women of the household, bring him fruit and flowers, touch his chin and play senet with him. It is tempting to connect these rooms with the harem conspiracy that ended his life, and some scholars think the attack took place somewhere in this complex. There is no proof, but these scenes show the world the plotters lived in.

Between this gate and the first pylon stand the chapels of the God's Wives of Amun, built five centuries later for royal princesses such as Amenirdis I and Shepenwepet II, who ruled Thebes as celibate high priestesses.
details: Under the windows: carved heads of foreign captives used as brackets.
Outer faces of the towers: Ramesses III smiting enemies before the gods.
The narrowing passage: built to funnel visitors, as in a real fortress.
Beyond the gate: the small stone chapels of the God's Wives of Amun.
fun_fact: Migdol shares its root with the Hebrew migdal, tower, which survives in the name of Magdala, the home town of Mary Magdalene.
narration: You are standing in the gatehouse of Medinet Habu, and it is built to look like a fortress. Ramesses the Third copied the shape from the fortified towers of Syria and Canaan, which were called migdol, a Semitic word for tower. Here it was mostly theatre, a stone poster for his wars. Look up at the windows. Underneath them, carved heads of foreign prisoners stick out of the wall, so anyone leaning on the sill rested their elbows on the king's enemies. The rooms upstairs were a private retreat, and their carvings are surprisingly intimate. The king sits while young women of his household bring him fruit and flowers, stroke his chin and play the board game senet with him. Some guides will tell you the plot to murder him was hatched up there. Nobody can prove it, but these scenes show the world the plotters lived in. Before you walk on, look at the small stone chapels between this gate and the temple. They belong to the God's Wives of Amun, royal princesses who ruled Thebes as high priestesses five centuries later.

period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, Ramesses III, year 8, c. 1175 BC
summary: The only detailed picture of a sea battle from the Bronze Age: Egyptian archers against the Sea Peoples, as the old Mediterranean world collapsed.
look: Walk round the outside of the temple's north wall: its reliefs run as one long campaign, from the Libyan wars to the Sea Peoples. The naval battle is a tangle of ships, with lion-head prows on the Egyptian side, bird-head prows at both ends of the enemy ships, and bodies in the water, while the huge figure of the king shoots from the shore. Inside, on the back wall of the first court north of the doorway, the long year 8 inscription names the invaders.
story:
Around 1200 BC the Bronze Age world of the eastern Mediterranean fell apart. Within a few decades the Hittite empire collapsed, the port of Ugarit was destroyed, and the Mycenaean palaces of Greece went up in flames. Drought, famine, earthquakes, revolts, broken trade and peoples on the move all played a part, and many historians now see the Sea Peoples as much refugees as raiders.

Egypt told it as an invasion. In year 8 of Ramesses III, about 1175 BC, the inscription here says, 'the foreign countries made a conspiracy in their islands'. It names them: the Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen and Weshesh. They came by land, with ox-carts full of women and children, and by sea. Ramesses claims he beat the land army in Djahy, on the coast of Canaan, and trapped the fleet in the mouths of the Nile, where hidden ships and archers overturned the enemy boats and dragged the men ashore.

The reliefs show warriors in feathered headdresses and others in horned helmets. Who were they? Most scholars think the Peleset settled on the coast of Canaan and became the Philistines of the Bible. The Denyen are tentatively linked with Homer's Danaans, the Sherden with Sardinia, the Shekelesh perhaps with Sicily; all of this is debated. Sherden warriors also served Egypt as hired soldiers, so they may appear on both sides.

Elsewhere on the walls, scribes count piles of hands and genitals cut from dead Libyans: the army's body count. Egypt survived, but within a century it had lost its empire in Canaan.
details: Outer north wall, naval battle: Egyptian prows end in a lion's head; the invaders' ships have bird heads at both ends.
Headgear: feathered headdresses of the Peleset and their allies, and warriors in horned helmets.
Capsized enemy boats and men being hauled out of the water as prisoners.
Land battle scenes: ox-carts carrying women and children, a migration, not just a raid.
First court, back wall north of the doorway: the long year 8 inscription naming the five peoples.
fun_fact: The Peleset of these reliefs most probably gave their name, through the Philistines, to the region later called Palestine.
narration: On this wall is a picture of the end of a world. Around 1200 BC the Bronze Age kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean collapsed. The Hittite empire fell, the great port of Ugarit was destroyed, and in Greece the Mycenaean palaces went up in flames. Drought, famine, earthquakes and whole peoples on the move all played a part. In year 8 of Ramesses the Third, about 1175 BC, a coalition the Egyptians described as coming from the islands headed for Egypt, by land with ox-carts full of families, and by sea. The texts name them: the Peleset, the Tjeker, the Shekelesh, the Denyen and the Weshesh. Ramesses claims he trapped their fleet in the mouths of the Nile. This is the only detailed picture of a sea battle to survive from the Bronze Age. Egyptian ships have a lion's head on the prow. The invaders' ships have a bird's head at each end. Archers fire volleys, boats capsize, and men tumble into the water to be fished out as prisoners. Who were these people? Most scholars think the Peleset settled on the coast of Canaan and became the Philistines. Some link the Denyen with Homer's Danaans, the Greeks at Troy. Now find the warriors in horned helmets. They are probably Sherden, and since Sherden also fought for Egypt as hired soldiers, they may be on both sides of this battle.

period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, c. 1186-1155 BC; church of Djeme, 5th-7th centuries AD
summary: Two courts in a row: one where the king leaned out of a window to hand out gold, and one where the original paint still glows.
look: Through the first pylon, the first court has statues of the king as Osiris against square pillars on your right, and columns on your left, where the Window of Appearances opens from the palace. Through the second pylon, the second court is ringed by more pillars and columns, with the best colour in the temple on its ceilings and walls. Beyond lie the roofless hypostyle hall, side rooms and the sanctuaries.
story:
The first court was the king's stage. On its south side the Window of Appearances connected to the mud-brick palace next door, used on festival days. Here the king showed himself to the court and rewarded loyal officials with gold collars. Behind the window you can walk into the palace ruins: a columned hall leading to an audience room with its throne platform, private rooms and baths. Theodore Davis's digging in 1913 damaged much of it. On the back wall of this court is the long inscription of year 8 about the Sea Peoples.

The second court was the heart of the temple's festivals. Its walls show the Feast of Min, god of fertility, with priests carrying statues of earlier kings, and the Feast of Sokar, god of the dead. On the east wall, in the upper register, sixteen cartouches name nine kings, a little king list. Along the back of the court, long processions of the king's sons line both sides of the doorway; their names were added later, probably under Ramesses IV, V or VI.

Some of the colour may owe its survival to Christians. In the 5th to 7th centuries the town of Djeme built a five-aisled church in this court. The builders cut away the Osiris statues from the pillars, which did not suit a church, and plastered the walls. Archaeologists cleared the church in the 19th century, without recording it properly.

Beyond, the hypostyle hall has lost its roof and the upper parts of its columns, but the side rooms still show the king presenting treasures to Amun.
details: First court, left (south) side: the Window of Appearances, opening from the palace.
Second court: tilt your head back for the blue ceilings with yellow stars.
Second court pillars: flat, chopped faces where Christian builders removed the Osiris statues.
Second court, east wall, upper register: the procession of Min with a row of royal cartouches.
Back of the second court: rows of princes either side of the doorway.
fun_fact: When the Chicago team arrived in the 1920s, the rubbish mounds of the Christian town stood 3 to 6 m high around the temple.
narration: You are in the first court, the king's stage. On your left, the south side, is a balcony opening called the Window of Appearances. Behind that wall stood the palace. On festival days Ramesses the Third stepped out here, showed himself to his court and rewarded loyal officials with collars of gold. Through a doorway on that side you can still walk into the mud-brick palace ruins and find the platform where his throne stood. On your right, the king stands as Osiris against each pillar, arms crossed, waiting for eternity. Now go through the second pylon into the second court, and look up. This is some of the best-preserved temple colour in Egypt: blue ceilings with yellow stars, painted column tops, kings in white linen. On the walls, priests carry statues of earlier kings in the festival of Min, god of fertility, and the boat of Sokar, god of the dead, comes out in procession. Part of that colour may have survived thanks to Christians. Around 1,500 years ago the town of Djeme built a church in this court. The builders hacked the statues off the pillars to make plain columns and plastered over the walls. Find a pillar here with its statue chopped flat: that is the church builders' work, and the paint beside it is more than 3,000 years old.

summary: A queen, her son, palace officials and wax figures: the murder of Ramesses III, confirmed 3,000 years later by a CT scanner.
look: Nothing here is labelled 'murder'. Walk to the palace ruins along the south side of the first court, the household world where the plot was born. The documents of the trial are in Turin, and the mummies of both the king and the probable plotter prince are at the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in Cairo.
story:
Ramesses III had many wives. One of them, a secondary queen named Tiye, wanted her son Pentawer on the throne instead of the chosen heir, the future Ramesses IV. In 1155 BC she drew in officials from all over the palace. Pebekkamen, a chief of the chamber, organised the plot; a butler helped; an overseer of cattle obtained help from the overseer of the treasury to get past the harem's restricted access; harem officials, scribes and army officers joined. Messages went out to 'stir up the people' so that revolt would break out as the king died. The attack may have taken place at Medinet Habu during a festival.

The Judicial Papyrus of Turin records the trials, held as if ordered by the king himself. The plotters appear under 'names of infamy': a man called Mersure, 'Ra loves him', is written as 'Ra hates him'. Ramesses IV appointed twelve judges. Some 28 people were executed, and others, Pentawer among them, were allowed to take their own lives. Then came a scandal: two judges and a police captain had been socialising with the accused women, and they lost their noses and ears.

Did the plot succeed? For a century, scholars thought not. Then a CT scan published in 2012 showed the king's throat cut to the bone, a wound no one could survive; the embalmers had placed an Eye of Horus amulet in it. A later study found his left big toe chopped off, perhaps by an axe.

And Pentawer? Among the royal mummies is Unknown Man E, the 'Screaming Mummy', buried unembalmed in a ritually impure goatskin in an uninscribed coffin. DNA shows he was a son of Ramesses III, so he is probably Pentawer.
details: Palace ruins, south side of the first court: the throne platform where the royal household gathered.
The Migdol gate's upper rooms: the king with the women of his household.
On the walls of the second court: processions of the king's sons, rivals in the succession.
fun_fact: The court scribes punished the plotters in ink too: in the trial records, a man named 'Ra loves him' was renamed 'Ra hates him'.
narration: This temple belonged to a murdered king. Ramesses the Third had many wives. One of them, a secondary queen called Tiye, wanted her son Pentawer on the throne instead of the chosen heir. In 1155 BC she built a conspiracy: palace stewards, a butler, a treasury official, harem women, scribes and army officers. The plan was to kill the king and start a revolt outside the palace at the same moment. We know this from the trial records, above all the Judicial Papyrus of Turin. The scribes even renamed the plotters: a man called Ra loves him became Ra hates him. Dozens were condemned, and some, Pentawer among them, were allowed to take their own lives. Then came a scandal: two judges and a police captain had been partying with the accused women. They lost their noses and ears. For a century scholars argued whether the plot had worked. In 2012 a CT scan of the king's mummy answered: his throat had been cut deep, right to the bone. The embalmers placed an Eye of Horus amulet in the wound. And Pentawer? Among the royal mummies is a young man known as the Screaming Mummy, buried without proper rites, wrapped in a goatskin. DNA shows he was a son of Ramesses the Third. Both mummies are now in Cairo. Walk to the palace ruins beside the first court: this is the household where the plot was born.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1479-1425 BC, with additions to the Roman period
summary: Older and holier than everything around it: a small Amun temple on the mound where the gods of creation were believed to rest.
look: Just to the right as you come through the Migdol gate, a small temple sits behind later gateways and a forecourt added by Kushite, Saite, Ptolemaic and Roman rulers. The core is the 18th Dynasty shrine with its six-room sanctuary. Look for recut cartouches where Hatshepsut's name was replaced.
story: The temple was linked with the Ogdoad, the eight primeval gods of creation, believed to rest in a mound here. Hatshepsut began rebuilding it, claiming the old shrine had been neglected, but died before it was finished. Thutmose III completed it and removed her name. Every ten days, as most Egyptologists reconstruct it, Amun of Luxor crossed the river to make offerings to these ancestor gods. Later kings of the 20th, 25th, 26th, 29th and 30th Dynasties, and the Ptolemies and Romans after them, kept adding, so it was in use for some 1,500 years. Its holiness is one reason Ramesses III built his temple next door.
details: Inner sanctuary: cartouches of Thutmose III carved over Hatshepsut's erased names.
The front gateways: added by kings from Kush, Sais and the Ptolemies, over a thousand years after the core.
The sanctuary room with large statues of Amun and Thutmose III.
fun_fact: The temple was already old when Ramesses III arrived: about 300 years separate Hatshepsut's shrine from his temple next door.
narration: This small temple is older and holier than everything around it. It was linked with the eight gods of creation, who were believed to rest in a mound here. Hatshepsut began rebuilding it about 3,450 years ago, but died before it was finished. Thutmose the Third completed it and had her name removed. Every ten days, Amun of Luxor is thought to have crossed the river to make offerings to these ancestor gods. Later kings, from the Kushites to the Romans, kept adding gates and courts, so the building grew for some 1,500 years. That holiness is why Ramesses the Third built right next door. In the inner rooms, look for cartouches cut over Hatshepsut's erased name.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Ramesses II, c. 1279-1213 BC
summary: Ramesses II's own temple, where a shattered thousand-ton colossus gave Shelley his 'Ozymandias'.
look: Much of the first pylon and court are tumbled ruins. The fallen granite colossus lies in huge pieces near the second court: look for the head, the chest and a foot bigger than you. Beyond, Osiride pillars stand on the right side of the second court, then the hypostyle hall, where 39 of the 48 columns still stand. Vaulted mud-brick storerooms surround the temple on three sides.
story:
Ramesses II called it the 'House of millions of years of Usermaatra-setepenra that unites with Thebes-the-city in the domain of Amun'. It covers about 10 hectares. Champollion, who visited in 1829, gave it the name Rhamesseion.

The fallen giant was a seated colossus of Aswan granite, estimated at about 1,000 tons and up to 19 m tall, moved some 220 km from the quarry. In the 1st century BC the Greek historian Diodorus of Sicily called the place the tomb of Ozymandias, a Greek form of the king's throne name, and quoted its boast: 'King of Kings Ozymandias am I. If any want to know how great I am and where I lie, let him outdo me in my work.' Around Christmas 1817 Percy Bysshe Shelley turned that into a sonnet, published in January 1818. Giovanni Belzoni had already removed the Younger Memnon, a 6-ton granite head and torso from this temple, now in the British Museum.

The first pylon and the second court show the Battle of Kadesh. Diodorus also describes a sacred library with the words 'healing place of the soul' over its door. Around the temple, granaries and storerooms with some of the oldest true mud-brick vaults in Egypt held the temple's wealth, and a school trained scribes.
details: The fallen colossus: find the head, the chest and the giant foot, and look for the king's name in a cartouche.
First pylon and second court: the Battle of Kadesh, with the Hittites routed into the river.
Second court, right side: the surviving Osiride pillars of the king.
Hypostyle hall: patches of the gold-starred blue ceiling.
Behind the temple: long vaulted mud-brick storerooms, some of the oldest true arches in Egypt.
fun_fact: Shelley wrote 'Ozymandias' as a friendly sonnet contest with his friend Horace Smith, who published his own 'Ozymandias' a few weeks later. Nobody remembers Smith's.
narration: Welcome to the Ramesseum, the temple Ramesses the Second built for his own eternal cult. Find the huge granite fragments lying in the court. They are the remains of a seated colossus of the king, estimated at about 1,000 tons and up to 19 metres tall, one of the largest statues ever carved in Egypt. The Greek historian Diodorus of Sicily described this place more than 2,000 years ago as the tomb of Ozymandias, a Greek version of the king's throne name. He quoted a boast carved on the statue: King of kings Ozymandias am I. If any want to know how great I am and where I lie, let him outdo me in my work. Around Christmas 1817 the English poet Percy Bysshe Shelley turned that into a sonnet about the emptiness of power. Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair. Nothing beside remains. Look on the pylon for Ramesses at the Battle of Kadesh, his favourite story, and behind the temple for the vaulted mud-brick storerooms. Then go back to the fallen giant and find the foot: it is bigger than you.

period: Mostly New Kingdom, 18th-20th Dynasties, c. 1550-1070 BC
summary: Royal tombs show the gods; these officials' tombs show people: banquets, harvests, hunting trips and envoys from Crete.
look: The hillside of Sheikh Abd el-Qurna, between Deir el-Bahari and the Ramesseum, is pitted with doorways: these are the chapels of private tombs, many behind steel gates. Tickets come in small groups of two or three tombs, so decide which group you want before you buy. Most of the village houses that once covered the slope have been demolished.
story:
At least 415 private tombs on the West Bank carry a TT number, for Theban Tomb, and this hill has the greatest concentration. The numbers follow the order in which tombs were catalogued, from Gardiner and Weigall's list of 1913 onwards, not their position, which is why TT1 is at Deir el-Medina.

The famous ones here belong to the men who ran the empire in the 18th Dynasty: viziers, mayors, scribes and priests of Amun. A noble's tomb had two parts: a chapel cut into the hill, where the family came to bring offerings and remember the dead, and a shaft down to the burial. Because the chapel was meant for visitors, its walls show the life the owner hoped to continue: banquets with musicians, harvests, fishing and fowling in the marshes, workshops and foreign envoys with tribute.

For about two centuries the village of Qurna stood on top of the tombs, and some families lived partly inside them and made a living from what they found. In the late 2000s the authorities demolished most of the houses and moved the villagers to new settlements.

The usual groups: Rekhmire and Sennefer; Ramose, Userhat and Khaemhat; Nakht and Menna. If you can choose only one, take Nakht and Menna for colour, or Rekhmire for stories.
details: Doorways along the slope: each modern steel gate marks a numbered tomb chapel.
The domed tomb of the local saint, Sheikh Abd el-Qurna, who gave the hill its name.
Tomb courtyards cut into the slope in front of the doorways, where families once gathered with offerings.
Look back east: the Ramesseum and the green fields below, the view the nobles chose.
fun_fact: The tomb numbers record the order of cataloguing, not geography, so TT1 is in the workmen's village and TT100 is up here.
narration: This hillside is honeycombed with tombs. At least 415 private tombs on the West Bank carry a T T number, and this slope has the most. They belong to the men who ran Egypt's empire: viziers, mayors, scribes and priests of Amun. A royal tomb was sealed forever, but a noble's tomb had a chapel where the family came to bring food and remember the dead. Because it was meant for visitors, its walls show the life the owner wanted to continue: banquets with musicians, harvests, fishing trips and foreign envoys. The kings' tombs show the gods. These show people. For about two centuries a village called Qurna sat on top of the tombs. Families built their houses over the entrances. In the late 2000s most of the houses were demolished and the villagers were moved to new settlements. Tickets come in small groups of two or three tombs. If you can only choose one group, take Nakht and Menna for colour, or Rekhmire and Sennefer for stories. Look along the slope for doorways with modern steel gates: each one is a numbered tomb.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Thutmose III and Amenhotep II, 15th century BC
summary: A vizier's tomb that reads like an encyclopaedia of the empire: law, taxes, tribute from Crete and Nubia, and every craft in Thebes.
look: A wide, shallow hall about 21 m across, then a long corridor almost 27 m deep whose ceiling climbs from about 3.3 m to over 8 m at the far end. Tribute and the duties of the vizier fill the hall; workshops, the funeral and a banquet line the corridor, with a niche at the end.
story: Rekhmire was vizier, the chief minister, at the end of Thutmose III's reign and under Amenhotep II, and lists over a hundred titles. His walls spell out a vizier's duties: taxes, the treasury, appointments and impartial justice in line with Maat. In the hall, foreign envoys bring tribute: people of Punt, Keftiu from Crete with Minoan vases, Nubians with leopards and a giraffe, Syrians with chariots, horses, a bear and an elephant. In the corridor, craftsmen make bricks, cast metal, work leather, build furniture and carve a colossal statue. Then he fell from favour under Amenhotep II: his figures were erased, and his burial has never been found.
details: Hall: the Keftiu, men from Crete, carrying tall Minoan vases.
Hall: Nubians leading a giraffe, and Syrians with a small elephant and a bear.
Corridor: brickmakers, metalworkers, carpenters and sculptors at work on a colossus.
Rekhmire's own figures: many scraped away or painted over after his disgrace.
fun_fact: The corridor ceiling rises from about 3.3 m to over 8 m, unusual in these hills, so the far end feels like a small cathedral.
narration: You are in the tomb chapel of Rekhmire, vizier, which means chief minister, of Thutmose the Third and Amenhotep the Second. His walls are a handbook for running an empire. In this wide hall, foreign envoys bring tribute. Find the men from Crete, the Keftiu, carrying tall Minoan vases: the Aegean world as an Egyptian painter saw it. Nubians bring a giraffe and leopards, and Syrians bring horses, a bear and even a small elephant. Now walk down the long corridor and watch the ceiling rise to over 8 metres. Here are the workshops: brickmakers, metal casters and sculptors finishing a colossus. Then look at Rekhmire's own figures: many were scraped away. He fell from favour, and nobody knows why.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, reign of Amenhotep II, 15th century BC
summary: Down a steep tunnel, a burial chamber whose rough ceiling is painted as a grape arbour: the Tomb of the Vines.
look: A steep, low tunnel takes you down to a painted antechamber, then through a doorway guarded by jackals into a four-pillared burial chamber. The uneven rock ceiling was left unsmoothed and painted with vines and dark bunches of grapes, so the bumps look like real foliage. Meryt appears with Sennefer on the pillars.
story: Sennefer was mayor of Thebes under Amenhotep II, and his wife Meryt shares the tomb. What you visit is the burial chamber, reached by a steep tunnel. The painters turned the uneven ceiling into a grape arbour, eternal shade with a promise of wine. On the walls, the funeral procession sets out, the couple make the ritual boat journey to Abydos, and a priest purifies them. On the pillars, Meryt offers her husband myrrh, food and lotus flowers, and he sits in the shade of a tree. A Greco-Roman graffito shows the tomb was already open to visitors 2,000 years ago.
details: Ceiling: vines and bunches of grapes painted straight onto the bumpy rock.
Doorway into the burial chamber: the guardian jackals.
Pillars: Meryt offering lotus flowers and myrrh to her husband.
Sennefer's chest: the amulet of two hearts he wears on a cord.
fun_fact: The painters never smoothed this ceiling: they used the lumps in the rock as the volume of the leaves and grapes.
narration: Mind your head on the way down. You are in the burial chamber of Sennefer, mayor of Thebes under Amenhotep the Second, and of his wife Meryt. Now look up. The painters did not bother to smooth the rock. Instead they turned the bumpy ceiling into a grape arbour, with twisting vines and bunches of dark grapes, so that the couple would rest forever in cool shade. On the walls, the funeral procession sets out and the couple sail to the holy city of Abydos. On the pillars, Meryt offers her husband lotus flowers and myrrh, and he sits in the shade of a tree. Look closely at Sennefer's chest: he wears an amulet of two hearts on a cord.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Amenhotep III and early Akhenaten, c. 1350 BC
summary: One tomb, two art styles: classic reliefs on one wall, the new Amarna look on the other, abandoned when the court left for Amarna.
look: A large hall that once had 32 columns in four rows of eight, many now broken. On the east wall, either side of the entrance, delicate unpainted reliefs of Ramose and his family; on the west wall opposite, Akhenaten under a canopy and with Nefertiti at a balcony, partly only sketched. The painted funeral scenes are on the south wall.
story: Ramose was vizier, the king's chief minister, at the end of Amenhotep III's reign and the start of his son's. His sculptors began in the classic style: on the east wall, Ramose, his brother Amenhotep and Amenhotep's wife May sit in fine linen and braided wigs, carved with extraordinary precision and never painted. On the south wall, painted mourners follow the funeral. Then the new king, still called Amenhotep IV, changed everything. On the west wall he sits under a canopy with Maat beside him, and then leans from a balcony with Nefertiti to reward Ramose with gold, in the new style. Parts are only sketched. When the court moved to Amarna, work stopped, and the burial chamber seems never to have been used.
details: East wall: the unpainted reliefs of Ramose's family, with finely carved eyes and braided wigs.
West wall, left: the king enthroned in the old style, with conquered peoples below his throne.
West wall, right: the king and Nefertiti at a balcony, in the new style, rewarding Ramose with gold.
South wall: the painted procession of mourning women, arms raised.
fun_fact: The same patron, the same tomb, perhaps the same sculptors: you can watch Egyptian art change direction between one wall and the next.
narration: This tomb caught a revolution in the act. Ramose was vizier, the king's chief minister, under Amenhotep the Third and then his son, the future Akhenaten. Start on the wall either side of the entrance. Ramose, his brother and their wives sit in fine linen and braided wigs, carved in perfect classic style and never painted. Now turn to the wall opposite. On the left, the new king, still calling himself Amenhotep the Fourth, sits in the old style. On the right he leans from a balcony with Nefertiti, rewarding Ramose with gold, in the new style. Parts are only sketched. When the court moved to Amarna, the work simply stopped. Compare the faces on the two walls: two worlds in one room.
